overview: This map label fits the kingdom of Burgundy and Arles, linking the Rhône valley with lands around western Switzerland and Alpine passes. It is distinct from the duchy centred on Dijon. The imported outline is approximate and continues long after the independent royal dynasty ended.

periods.title: The Rudolfian kingdom
periods.summary: A northern kingdom expanded south into the Rhône lands. Royal authority competed with regional aristocrats and bishops.

periods.title: Burgundy within the Empire
periods.summary: After the dynasty ended, the kingdom passed to imperial rulers. Local powers continued to gain strength; 1279 is only this map record’s endpoint.

items.text: Control of Alpine passes made Burgundy valuable to emperors travelling toward Italy. Royal estates lay among counties, while bishops received political powers. The kingdom was held together through relationships, land and strategic roads rather than one uniform administration.

sections.title: A lakeside community around the year 1000

items.text: At Colletière beside Lake Paladru, early eleventh-century families lived inside a timber enclosure. Three wooden buildings, a workshop and livestock facilities survive archaeologically. Waterlogged conditions preserved wood, seeds and leather that would normally rot away, giving this small community an unusually clear material record.

Cereal grains, sickles, hooks, net floats and fish scales reveal farming and fishing. Animal bones show different foods in the main house and smaller buildings. Researchers interpret those differences as signs of social rank within the settlement, rather than a single menu shared by everyone.

Colletière also produced chess pieces and musical instruments, including a bowed instrument called a vielle. Its inhabitants had tools for weaving, carpentry and metalworking. Work filled much of life, but the surviving objects leave room for music and a board-game argument too.

A tiny leather shoe from Colletière belonged to a child. A small maple shoemaker’s last helped shape footwear for very young children. These objects put families into a story otherwise easily crowded with kings, mounted warriors and abbots.

Leather offcuts show that shoes were made locally. Oak cutting templates, metal awls and tools for threading laces reveal the stages of the craft. Different models and stitching methods suggest that medieval shoemakers cared about variety as well as keeping feet covered.

sections.title: Royal women and a growing monastery

items.text: At Payerne, the Burgundian royal family supported a religious community before the year 1000. Adelaide, daughter of Queen Bertha and herself an empress, connected it with the monastery of Cluny. Women in the dynasty helped shape institutions as well as royal family relationships.

Builders began Payerne’s great Romanesque church in the eleventh century. Later priors altered and embellished it. The standing building is therefore a layered achievement of masonry and patronage, not a church completed in one royal building season.

The Great Saint Bernard hospice is securely documented from 1125, with an earlier foundation traditionally placed around 1050. Its religious community assisted pilgrims crossing the Alps. Food, shelter and spiritual care belonged together at a route where reaching the other side was a serious undertaking.

By 1177 the hospice’s wider network counted 78 hospices, houses, priories and churches. Gifts and properties supported the work. The famous rescue dogs belong to much later evidence, so a medieval traveller should not automatically be pictured meeting one.

A charter dated 24 April 1011 names Neuchâtel as “Novum castellum”, meaning “new castle”. This is a Latin phrase preserved in the published transcription of Rudolf III’s gift to Queen Ermengarde. The original parchment survives in the Isère archives, with a royal wax seal.

The gift transferred revenues from royal estates, including the work of unfree peasants attached to them. A later note records Ermengarde’s donation to the church of Saint-Maurice in Vienne. The document links affection, property, labour and religion in one royal household’s decisions.

ending.text: Rudolf III died in 1032, ending the dynasty. Incorporation into the Empire unfolded through 1038. Burgundy retained a royal title, while regional lordships increasingly shaped everyday government. Its people and settlements continued beyond this political transition.
